title: Matplotlib Histograms and Frequency Distributions
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and core concepts of Matplotlib Histograms and Frequency Distributions.
Select suitable Python structures or library operations for the task.
Trace the effect of each operation on the data or figure.
Validate results and interpret output accurately.
Identify limitations, edge cases and maintainability considerations.

understand.concept: A histogram groups numeric observations into intervals called bins and displays the count or density in each interval. Bin edges and bin count affect the visible distribution, so they should be chosen deliberately. Histograms describe numeric distributions; they are not interchangeable with bar charts of unrelated categories.
understand.whyItMatters: Histograms help reveal spread, skew, clusters and possible outliers in numeric data.
understand.analogy: Choose the data structure or chart that matches the information being represented; visual similarity does not mean two structures have identical behavior.
understand.summary: Matplotlib Histograms and Frequency Distributions adds a focused capability to the Python curriculum.

explain.narrative: Read the concept, run each example in order, inspect the returned values and figure objects, and compare the result with the stated expectation. The examples use deterministic data and a non-interactive Matplotlib backend so they can be validated in automation.

examples.title: Create histogram bin counts
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
counts, edges, patches = ax.hist([1, 2, 2, 3], bins=[0, 2, 4])
print(counts.astype(int).tolist())
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: The chosen bins count one value in [0,2) and three in [2,4].

examples.title: Set an explicit number of bins
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
counts, edges, patches = ax.hist([1, 2, 3, 4], bins=2)
print(len(counts), len(edges))
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: Two bins require three boundary edges.

examples.title: Label a histogram
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist([2, 3, 3, 4], bins=3)
ax.set(title='Scores', xlabel='Score', ylabel='Frequency')
print(ax.get_title(), ax.get_ylabel())
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: Titles and axis labels explain what the bins represent.

examples.title: Use density normalization
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
counts, edges, patches = ax.hist([1, 2, 3, 4], bins=2, density=True)
print(round(sum(counts * (edges[1:] - edges[:-1])), 5))
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: For a density histogram, total bar area is one.

examples.title: Save a histogram image
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from io import BytesIO
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist([1, 1, 2, 3], bins=3)
buf = BytesIO(); fig.savefig(buf, format='png')
print(buf.getvalue()[:4] == b'\x89PNG')
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: A figure can be exported without opening a graphical window.
